findings.label: Troponin-I
findings.source: Contemporary (quantitative) cTnI: 0.04 ng/mL, the cut-off used in this project’s dataset (ml/README.md). Your lab’s 99th-percentile limit may differ.

findings.label: Systolic blood pressure
findings.source: 2017 ACC/AHA High Blood Pressure Guideline (Whelton et al., Hypertension 2018): normal <120, elevated 120–129, stage 1 130–139, stage 2 ≥140, crisis >180 mmHg. Low: <90 mmHg (AHA).

findings.label: Random blood sugar
findings.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2024: random glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) meets the diabetes criterion with symptoms; hypoglycemia level 1 <3.9, level 2 <3.0 mmol/L. 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) is the upper normal post-load value.

findings.label: Total cholesterol
findings.source: NCEP ATP III (NHLBI 2002): desirable <200, borderline high 200–239, high ≥240 mg/dL.

findings.label: LDL cholesterol
findings.source: NCEP ATP III: optimal <100, near optimal 100–129, borderline 130–159, high 160–189, very high ≥190 mg/dL.

findings.label: HDL cholesterol
findings.source: NCEP ATP III: low HDL <40 mg/dL in men and <50 mg/dL in women (metabolic syndrome criteria).

findings.label: Triglycerides
findings.source: NCEP ATP III: normal <150, borderline 150–199, high 200–499, very high ≥500 mg/dL.

findings.label: Hemoglobin
findings.source: WHO 2011 hemoglobin thresholds for anemia (non-pregnant adults): men <13, women <12 g/dL; mild 11–12.9 (men) / 11–11.9 (women), moderate 8–10.9, severe <8. Upper limit: typical lab reference (17.5 men, 15.5 women).

findings.label: Creatinine
findings.source: Typical lab reference 0.7–1.3 (men) / 0.6–1.1 (women) mg/dL. Severity from eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021, race-free) using KDIGO 2012 categories: G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15 mL/min/1.73m².

findings.label: Platelets
findings.source: Typical lab reference 150–400 ×10³/µL (MedlinePlus). Low grades from CTCAE v5.0 platelet count decreased: grade 1 <150–75, grade 2 <75–50, grade 3–4 <50.

findings.label: Sodium
findings.source: Reference 135–145 mmol/L. Hyponatremia grades from the European clinical practice guideline (Spasovski et al., 2014): mild 130–135, moderate 125–129, profound <125. Hypernatremia grades from CTCAE v5.0: grade 1 >145–150, grade 2 >150–155, grade 3 >155–160, grade 4 >160 mmol/L.

findings.label: Potassium
findings.source: Typical reference 3.5–5.1 mmol/L. Hyperkalemia grades from the European Resuscitation Council 2021 (mild 5.5–5.9, moderate 6.0–6.4, severe ≥6.5); hypokalemia: mild 3.0–3.4, moderate 2.5–2.9, severe <2.5.

findings.label: Chloride
findings.source: Typical lab reference 98–107 mmol/L. Interpreted with sodium; no separate severity grading is used.

findings.label: Body mass index
findings.source: WHO adult BMI classification. For Asian populations WHO also gives lower public-health action points (23 and 27.5 kg/m²), not applied here.

findings.source: Established major risk factor (ACC/AHA 2019 Primary Prevention Guideline).

sections.title: When to talk to a doctor

items.text: Nothing here needs a doctor right now. Keep up regular health check-ups.
Base meals on vegetables, fruit, whole grains, pulses and unsalted nuts and seeds. Choose vegetable oils over ghee or butter, and limit fried and processed food.
items.source: AHA 2021 Dietary Guidance to Improve Cardiovascular Health

items.text: Build up to 150–300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking, cycling, swimming), such as 30 minutes on 5 days. Start with 10-minute walks and add a few minutes each week.
Add muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week (bodyweight squats, resistance bands, light weights).
Break up long periods of sitting: stand up or walk for a few minutes every 30–60 minutes.
If you smoke or use tobacco, quitting is the most effective step for your heart.
Aim for 7–9 hours of sleep a night.
Manage stress with regular activity, breathing exercises and time with people you trust.

sections.title: When to talk to a doctor

items.text: Mention your total cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides, BMI, diagnosed hypertension and family history of heart disease at your next routine check-up.
Follow a DASH-style eating pattern: plenty of vegetables, fruit, pulses, whole grains and low-fat dairy. In trials it lowered systolic pressure by about 11 mmHg in people with hypertension.
because: Blood pressure 132 mmHg · Stage 1 hypertension range
items.source: NHLBI DASH eating plan; 2017 ACC/AHA guideline

items.text: Cut salt: aim for under 1,500 mg of sodium a day, or at least 1,000 mg less than now. Skip added salt, pickles, chips and instant noodles.
because: Blood pressure 132 mmHg · Stage 1 hypertension range

items.text: Keep saturated fat under 6% of calories: swap ghee, butter, coconut oil, fatty red meat and full-fat dairy for vegetable oils, fish, pulses and low-fat dairy.
Add soluble fibre every day: oats, barley, lentils, beans, okra and apples all help lower LDL.
Eat fish twice a week, ideally oily fish such as sardine, mackerel or hilsa.
Limit added sugar to under 36 g a day (sweets, sugary drinks, desserts), and keep portions of white rice and refined flour small.
Avoid alcohol: it raises triglycerides.
Aim to lose 5–10% of your weight (about 4–7 kg) over 6 months, with a modest deficit of about 500 kcal a day.
Base meals on vegetables, fruit, whole grains, pulses and unsalted nuts and seeds. Choose vegetable oils over ghee or butter, and limit fried and processed food.
items.source: AHA 2021 Dietary Guidance to Improve Cardiovascular Health

items.text: Build up to 150–300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking, cycling, swimming), such as 30 minutes on 5 days. Start with 10-minute walks and add a few minutes each week.
Regular aerobic exercise lowers systolic blood pressure by about 5–8 mmHg: it’s one of the most effective non-drug steps.
because: Blood pressure 132 mmHg · Stage 1 hypertension range

items.text: Add muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week (bodyweight squats, resistance bands, light weights). Breathe out as you lift, and avoid heavy lifting or holding your breath.
because: Blood pressure 132 mmHg · Stage 1 hypertension range

items.text: Break up long periods of sitting: stand up or walk for a few minutes every 30–60 minutes.
If you smoke or use tobacco, quitting is the most effective step for your heart.
Check your blood pressure at home: sit quietly for 5 minutes, arm supported at heart level, take 2 readings a minute apart, and keep a log to show your doctor.
because: Blood pressure 132 mmHg · Stage 1 hypertension range

items.text: Recheck your lipid profile after about 3 months of changes, as your doctor advises.
Aim for 7–9 hours of sleep a night.
Manage stress with regular activity, breathing exercises and time with people you trust.

groups.title: Heart muscle marker
groups.why: Troponin-I is released when heart muscle is injured. A result above the assay’s reference limit needs prompt medical review, whatever the model’s estimate says.
findings: Troponin-I 850 ng/L · Above the 99th-percentile limit (possible heart muscle injury)

groups.title: Blood pressure
groups.why: Raised blood pressure strains the heart and arteries over time. It is one of the strongest modifiable causes of heart disease and stroke.
findings: Blood pressure 185 mmHg · Hypertensive crisis range

groups.title: Blood sugar
groups.why: High blood sugar damages blood vessels over time, and diabetes roughly doubles the risk of heart disease. Very low blood sugar is dangerous in the short term.
findings: Blood sugar 14.5 mmol/L · Diabetes-range random glucose

groups.title: Cholesterol & triglycerides
groups.why: LDL cholesterol builds up in artery walls (atherosclerosis). Low HDL and high triglycerides add to that risk.

groups.title: Kidney function
groups.why: Reduced kidney function is linked to higher cardiovascular risk, and it changes which foods and medicines are safe.
findings: Creatinine 1.90 mg/dL · eGFR 38: Moderately to severely decreased (G3b)

groups.title: Reported history
groups.why: These are established risk factors or symptoms rather than measurements. Chest pain in particular should always be discussed with a clinician.

groups.title: Electrolytes
groups.why: Sodium, potassium and chloride keep fluid balance and the heartbeat steady. Potassium that is too high or too low can disturb heart rhythm.

groups.title: Blood count
groups.why: Low hemoglobin (anemia) makes the heart work harder to deliver oxygen. Abnormal platelet counts affect bleeding and clotting.

groups.title: Body weight
groups.why: Excess weight raises blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar. Being underweight can reflect poor nutrition or illness.

sections.title: When to talk to a doctor

items.text: Contact a doctor today about the raised Troponin-I. If you have chest pain or pressure, breathlessness, sweating or fainting now, call emergency services.
because: Troponin-I 850 ng/L · Above the 99th-percentile limit (possible heart muscle injury)
items.source: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)

items.text: Blood pressure above 180 mmHg: rest for 5 minutes and measure again. If it’s still that high, or you have chest pain, severe headache, vision changes, weakness or trouble speaking, get emergency care.
because: Blood pressure 185 mmHg · Hypertensive crisis range

items.text: Chest pain should be evaluated by a clinician, especially pain that comes on with exertion or at rest.
Your sodium is low: don’t cut salt further or drink large amounts of water to “flush” your system until a doctor has looked at the cause.
Book an appointment to review your cardiovascular risk and these results with a doctor.
Discuss your blood sugar, total cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides and creatinine with a doctor soon.

A DASH-style diet usually helps blood pressure, but it’s rich in potassium. Check with your doctor first, given your potassium or kidney result.

Use the plate method: half non-starchy vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter whole grains or pulses, at regular meal times.

Avoid protein powders and very high-protein diets, keep salt down, and ask before using potassium-based salt substitutes.
